name: Acute triangle
seoDesc: Acute triangle: work out area (More triangle data) from the angle β and the angle γ. A free math calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Acute triangle calculator turns the angle β, the angle γ and the side b into area (More triangle data). Think of it as a shortcut for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Acute triangle calculator work?
sections.html:
The Acute triangle calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports area (More triangle data) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the angle β, the angle γ, the side b and the side c.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Acute triangle calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Area=((1 ÷ 4) × the square root of (-(side a ^ 4) + 2 × (side a ^ 2) × (side b ^ 2) + 2 × (side a ^ 2) × (side c ^ 2) − (side b ^ 4) + 2 × (side b ^ 2) × (side c ^ 2) − (side c ^ 4)))
Angle α=(((1 ÷ 2) × (-(side a ^ 2) + (side b ^ 2) + (side c ^ 2)) ÷ (side b × side c)))
Angle β=(((1 ÷ 2) × ((side a ^ 2) − (side b ^ 2) + (side c ^ 2)) ÷ (side a × side c)))
Angle γ=(-(((1 ÷ 2) × ((side a ^ 2) − (side b ^ 2) + (side c ^ 2)) ÷ (side a × side c))) − (((1 ÷ 2) × (-(side a ^ 2) + (side b ^ 2) + (side c ^ 2)) ÷ (side b × side c))) + PI)
Perimeter=(side a + side b + side c)
Side c=(the square root of ((side a ^ 2) − 2 × side a × side b × the cosine of (angle γ) + (side b ^ 2)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Given set to three angles (AAA), Side a = 30 cm, Side b = 30 cm and Side c = 30 cm. Working through the relationship above gives Angle α = 60 deg, Angle β = 60 deg, Angle γ = 60 deg and Side c = 5.2293 cm.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Angle α = 60 deg, Angle β = 60 deg, Angle γ = 60 deg and Side c = 5.2293 cm should be roughly the size you expected from Given set to three angles (AAA) and Side a = 30 cm.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Acute triangle calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the angle β, the angle γ and the side b — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Acute triangle calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns area (More triangle data), derived from the angle β, the angle γ and the side b. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Acute triangle calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the angle β, the angle γ and the side b, which is 12 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter angle α in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Angle α opens in degrees and the chip beside it offers 12 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Angle α = 60 deg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Acute triangle calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
